item.title: AI stocks retreat as Democratic sweep puts data centre boom in focus
item.description: AI-related stocks came under pressure on Wednesday despite a broader Wall Street rally following the Democratic sweep of Congress. Data centre companies CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius fell, alongside Nvidia and Marvell, as investors weighed concerns over rising power costs, job losses, political scrutiny and debt-funded AI spending.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Wall Street's rally following the Democratic sweep of Congress did not extend to several companies riding the AI boom. Data centre builders and related technology stocks fell on Wednesday as investors weighed the possibility of greater political scrutiny of the industry's rapid expansion, Bloomberg reports.CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius declined, while power equipment makers GE Vernova and Vertiv also came under pressure. Chipmakers Nvidia and Marvell Technology slipped even as the Nasdaq 100 rose more than 1%.For live updates on US Markets, click here The election has brought concerns about rising electricity bills and AI-driven job losses into sharper focus. Meanwhile, investors were already questioning whether the industry's debt-fuelled spending can be sustained. According to Bloomberg, analysts do not expect political pressure to derail AI development, it could slow the pace of data centre expansion and investment.Also Read: Democrats’ Senate win could shield Federal Reserve from Trump’s influence, but risks persist“The Democrats will not in my opinion challenge what has already been implemented to win this race when it comes to AI. Because there is now a big competition between China and the US when it comes to technology,” Mabrouk Chetouane, Head of Global Market Strategy at Natixis Investment Managers, told Bloomberg.“Some of the questions on data centers suggested concerns about regulation should be faded, but others suggested they should remain in the spotlight. Regardless of what does or does not happen with Congress on this issue, risk does remain from the governors’ results as AI/data centers was a top issue in the close campaigns for those seats,” Lori Calvasina, Head of US Equity Strategy at RBC Capital Markets, said.“We still struggle to support the idea that the election will be a major clearing event for markets, however, given the absence of the usual turbulence in the US equity market around the election so far.”“This does add uncertainty about the path forward and maybe the pace forward, but ultimately we still think that the data center build-out will continue. Maybe the pace changes on the margin, but we ultimately think there’s huge demand for compute and that there may be some changes in how the data centers have to approach this, meaning maybe some of the tax incentives change, maybe some of the counties that really voted against this, maybe they have to move, go somewhere else. They might have to find other alternatives. But we think ultimately — much like fracking — we still expect that we see a buildout. It just may be done with some different concessions, with some guardrails, more guardrails than we had before,” Kieth Lerner, Chief Investment Officer and Chief Market Strategist at Truist Advisory Services, was quoted as saying by Bloomberg.“Republicans or Democrats sitting in any state around the country, not just Texas, look at a state that historically has been Republican friendly with a largely effective governor, seeing them overthrown on this basis that data centers are an unpopular position. I think politicians, if anything, love to get reelected before they think about policy. And so more and more, whether it be Republican or Democrat, are likely to jump on that bandwagon to air quotes protect their state from data centers. Obviously that is a popular narrative,” Brad Long, Chief Investment Officer at Wealthspire, said.“It’s certainly not going to change the fact that data centers will be built out and there’s a lot of demand and there’s a lot of backlog. The question will be the regulation and the time and the throughput there. What markets are going to have to digest is, it’s not will data centers be built, but where and how long will it take and how much red tape will be there? Which obviously pushes further out not just all the capex spending, but the throughput on the benefit from AI,” said Matt Maley, Chief Market Strategist at Miller Tabak + Co.“The headwinds are getting a little bit bigger for the AI movement. That’s going to give us some tough sledding. So it may be a lot harder for the market to see the usual year-end rally in the midterm election years. The ‘not in my backyard’ with data centers is gonna be a 2028 issue immediately, and I think that the 2028 campaign starts today. ... It is all but impossible for the Republicans to win the presidency or win the Electoral College without winning Texas,” he added.“Narrative-wise, I think the initial ‘Glass Half-Full’ post ‘Blue Tsunami’ midterm Elections -trade is based upon the following rationalizations—some probably obvious, some more nuanced: A belief that the election results will lead to a forced moderation of US datacenter buildout, which then calms concerns around the Hyperscaler Capex race-to-infinity ‘prisoner’s dilemma’…Which from a markets-perspective reduces some of financing concerns around magnitude of credit and equities issuance, slows the “FCF burn” -trajectory fears,” said Charlie McElligott, Cross Asset Strategist at Nomura Holdings Inc.“There’s definitely some fears about what this might mean for the AI build-out, especially on data centers, and those names have already been under pressure because of the expected Democratic victory. But I think it’s probably a little bit overblown. It’s going to put more onus on the states, but I don’t think that that will impact existing projects all that much. But it could result in higher cost of production if these companies have to provide maybe more local assistance or navigate more regulation across the board just to get some of these projects through. But we still need these data centers,” JP Powers, Chief Investment Officer at RWA Wealth Partners, told Bloomberg.“You could read this as a vote against data centers, but at some level there’s a lot of momentum toward building them, there’s a lot of jobs at stake. The boulder’s already rolling down the hill to some extent, so the election of a few governors and a change in Congress is not going to completely stop the momentum,” Steve Sosnick, Chief Strategist at Interactive Brokers, said.“The market’s been expressing very valid fears that the money is just being spent too aggressively and that the borrowing is so extreme. And so maybe this slows it down to something that’s a bit more manageable, which isn’t great for the suppliers, but may actually impose a little financial discipline on the industry that markets are okay with.”“This is a wake up call. They have to really get out and make their case why communities should want data centers. I think in the end they will be successful, but it probably slows some of these projects down,” Peter Tchir, Head of Macro Strategy at Academy Securities, said.“Gov-elect Hinojosa favors an immediate moratorium on data center builds in Texas until new laws can be passed to establish guardrails. One interpretation is that existing builds / permits would be free to continue and all new construction would be halted and thus would move to other states. Another interpretation is that the datacenter build is slowing and likely reducing capex; this theme had been building into the election,” Andrew Tyler, Head of Global Market Intelligence at JPMorgan Chase & Co., told Bloomberg. “We would not abandon the Tech trade and would play for a tactical rebound, but we may see the market become increasingly selective of Tech / AI winners and losers.” (Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: Democrats’ Senate win could shield Federal Reserve from Trump’s influence, but risks persist
item.description: Democrats’ midterm victory could strengthen the Federal Reserve’s independence by limiting President Donald Trump’s ability to appoint allies to its board. A Democrat controlled Senate could also intensify scrutiny of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, with Elizabeth Warren likely to lead the Senate Banking Committee and challenge the administration’s banking reforms.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory could strengthen the Federal Reserve’s ability to resist President Donald Trump’s attempts to influence monetary policy, with their expected control of the Senate emerging as a key obstacle to his efforts to reshape the central bank, Reuters reported.Control of the upper chamber gives Democrats significant leverage over Fed appointments, potentially making it harder for Trump to install allies on the central bank’s seven member board. However, the political shift could also bring greater scrutiny of Chairman Kevin Warsh and complicate the administration’s efforts to overhaul banking regulations.For live updates on US Markets, click here Senate control puts Trump’s Fed appointments under pressureThe change in political balance could significantly limit Trump’s ability to influence the Fed through appointments. Three of the central bank’s seven governors were appointed by former President Joe Biden, while former Chair Jerome Powell remains on the board despite his growing differences with Trump.Also Read: US stocks rally after Democrats' midterm sweep as AI infrastructure stocks slideTrump has repeatedly criticised the current composition of the board, calling it hostile and partisan , while pressing policymakers to cut interest rates. The Fed, however, has prioritised controlling inflation, Reuters reported.The Senate’s role in confirming nominees could become particularly important if Trump succeeds in removing Governor Lisa Cook. His administration is expected to pursue an administrative procedure in the coming weeks to establish grounds for her dismissal over alleged errors in mortgage applications filed before she joined the Fed.Cook is likely to challenge any removal in court. Even if Trump succeeds, a Democrat controlled Senate would make it difficult for him to secure confirmation of a replacement.Warsh faces tougher scrutiny as Warren gains influenceThe political shift could also make Warsh’s position more challenging. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren is likely to take charge of the Senate Banking Committee, replacing Republican Tim Scott, a Trump ally and supporter of Warsh.Warren has been a vocal critic of Warsh and could intensify scrutiny of his financial disclosures, including his handling of hundreds of millions of dollars in assets before taking the Fed’s top job.Democrats could also question his approach to inflation and monetary policy, particularly after campaigning heavily on the cost of living.Economists at Monetary Policy Analytics said Warsh got no support for his chairmanship from Democrats... Hostile questioning could put Warsh's rhetoric to the test .Meanwhile, Democratic control of key congressional committees could slow banking and regulatory changes backed by the administration and Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman, including stablecoin rules under the Genius Act and changes to the Fed's bank supervision framework, Reuters reported.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: AI data center stocks dip, renewables surge after Democrat sweep in US midterm elections
item.description: AI data centre stocks declined while renewable energy and healthcare shares rallied after Democrats won control of Congress in the US midterm elections. Investors assessed the possibility of tighter AI oversight and continued clean energy support. Defence contractors and prison operators fell amid concerns over changing government spending and immigration policies.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Data center stocks slid on Wednesday, while clean-energy shares rallied after Democrats seized control of Congress, prompting investors to reposition for tougher scrutiny of the AI boom and a shift in policy priorities.The Democratic sweep, which included victories in traditional Republican strongholds and key data-center hubs Texas and Georgia, will usher in divided government in Washington and raises the prospect of greater congressional oversight of industries that benefited from Republican control.Market reaction rippled across AI-linked stocks, renewables, healthcare companies, defense contractors and prison operators.DATA CENTER STOCKSData center operators lost ground, with Core Scientific down 3.5% and Iren down 3.6%. Applied Digital and CoreWeave fell 2.4% and 3.8%, respectively.The data center boom sparked public backlash this year, raising concerns that tighter Democratic oversight could slow investment just as investors grow wary of soaring AI spending and uncertain returns.Though analysts doubt any legislation could meaningfully stall data center construction, a Democratic-led Congress increases prospects of more hearings and investigations related to the AI buildout. AI has been an enormous engine powering the US economy, so any curbs on its future development could threaten to put the brakes on growth, said Kit Rees, investment strategist at Quilter.CLEAN ENERGYA Democratic sweep could bolster expectations for continued federal support for clean energy while speeding approvals for energy and infrastructure projects.Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration's efforts to roll back emissions rules and could use the Congressional Review Act to overturn regulations that make it easier to sell gas-powered trucks and SUVs.Shares of solar maker First Solar gained 7%, residential solar installer Sunrun added 6.1% and inverter maker Enphase Energy was up 3.6%. Clean-power developer NextEra Energy inched 2.3% higher. The more that oil and gas prices rise, the bigger the incentive, the bigger the economic incentive to roll out clean energy, said Paul Jackson, global market strategist for EMEA at Invesco.Europe's Vestas and Orsted rose 4.3% and 6.4%, respectively, while Portugal's EDP Renewables was up 2.3%.ELON MUSK-LED COMPANIESShares of Elon Musk's rocket and space technology company SpaceX dropped 5.2%, while EV maker Tesla was down 4.9%. It puts into doubt a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla. While Congress cannot stop a merger, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny, said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. Musk had poured hundreds of millions into the Republican Party ahead of these elections...we could see stocks linked to Musk struggle now that his political enemies have won back control of Congress. Trump Media & Technology Group, majority-owned by Trump, dropped 7.7%.DEFENSE STOCKSDefense contractors such as Northrop Grumman fell 2.7%, while RTX, Lockheed Martin and L3Harris lost over 2% each. The sector had been underpinned by expectations that the $1.5-trillion budget request by Trump would not face headwinds in a Republican-dominated Congress.However, in a Democrat-led Congress, analysts project the funding could fall short of expectations.HEALTH INSURERS AND HOSPITAL OPERATORSShares of hospital operators such as HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services gained 5.4% and 3.4%, respectively.Insurers such as Centene rose 4.7% and Elevance was marginally higher.Democrats have pushed for universal healthcare policies that could mean more government spending allocated to the sector.BNP Paribas economist Anis Bensaidani said Democrats may lack the numbers to pass legislation restoring major parts of the Affordable Care Act, but they could still win concessions while negotiating over defense spending and government funding.PRISON OPERATORSPrison operators such as GEO Group and CoreCivic fell 6.2% and 5.7%, respectively. The two stocks have rallied sharply since Trump won the presidency two years ago, as his clampdown on illegal immigration boosted the need for detention facilities.
